question: What do we call a tumor that has traveled to the brain from another part of the body, like the lungs?
explanation: You've got this! When cancer cells break away from a spot like the breast or lungs and travel to the brain, we call it a metastatic (or secondary) tumor. Think of it as a traveler from another part of the body.

question: Even if a brain tumor is benign (non-cancerous), why can it still turn into a medical emergency?

options.A: The immune system attacks the tumor and causes severe swelling.
options.B: The rigid skull prevents expansion and causes dangerous pressure.
options.C: Benign tumors always turn into fast-growing cancers over time.
options.D: Benign brain tumors immediately destroy all local nerve cells.

explanation: Great thinking! The human skull is like a hard box that cannot stretch. Even a benign growth takes up precious space inside, crowding the brain and causing dangerous pressure. Location matters just as much as cell type!

question: Most primary brain tumors start growing from which type of supportive cells in the nervous system?
explanation: Spot on! While neurons get all the fame for sending nerve signals, most primary brain tumors actually arise from glial cells—the supportive glue and caretaker cells of the brain.

question: A patient is diagnosed with a slow-growing, usually benign tumor that develops from the protective membranes covering the brain. What is it called?
explanation: You got it! Meningiomas grow from the meninges—the protective layers surrounding your brain and spinal cord. They are usually slow-growing and benign, which is great news for the patient.

question: During an eye exam, what classic sign tells a doctor there is increased pressure inside the skull?
explanation: Brilliant! Papilledema is simply the swelling of the optic nerve head. Because the optic nerve connects directly to the brain, high intracranial pressure pushes on it and shows up clearly during an eye check.

question: Which set of vital signs makes up the famous 'Cushing triad', warning us of severe brainstem compression?

options.A: Normal blood pressure, irregular pulse, and clear breath sounds
options.B: High fever, fast heart rate, and deep rapid respirations
options.C: Widening pulse pressure, slow heart rate, and irregular breathing
options.D: Low blood pressure, rapid pulse, and shallow breathing

explanation: You're doing great! The Cushing triad is a critical late warning sign. Watch out for a wide gap between top and bottom blood pressure numbers, a slow heart rate (bradycardia), and irregular breathing. It means the brainstem is in trouble!

question: Which imaging test is the absolute go-to choice for getting a clear picture of brain and spinal tumors?
explanation: Spot on! MRI gives doctors the sharpest, most detailed look at soft tissues like the brain and spinal cord, making it the favorite tool for spotting nervous system growths.

question: A patient asks how doctors will know for sure if a brain tumor is cancerous. What procedure gives the definitive diagnosis?
explanation: You nailed it! A biopsy is the gold standard. By looking at actual tumor cells under a microscope, pathologists can tell for sure if it's cancerous and figure out its grade.

question: Why do doctors frequently prescribe corticosteroid medications to patients with brain tumors?

options.A: To reduce brain swelling and intracranial pressure
options.B: To cure the underlying cancer cells completely
options.C: To lower the patient's blood pressure levels
options.D: To prevent the patient from developing an infection

explanation: Well done! Steroids like dexamethasone are lifesavers here. They don't kill the cancer, but they quickly shrink the puffy swelling (edema) around the tumor, bringing relief fast.

question: What is the biggest hurdle when trying to treat brain tumors using regular systemic chemotherapy drugs?

options.A: Chemotherapy drugs only work on bones and muscles.
options.B: Chemotherapy causes permanent blindness in every patient.
options.C: Brain tissue absorbs too much medication and dissolves instantly.
options.D: The blood-brain barrier blocks many drugs from entering the brain tissue.

explanation: You got it! The blood-brain barrier is like a strict security guard—it protects the brain from toxins, but unfortunately, it also blocks many helpful chemotherapy drugs from getting inside.

question: How should you position a patient right after a craniotomy surgery to help keep intracranial pressure down?

options.B: Flat on the back with feet raised high
options.D: Lying flat on the operative side

explanation: Excellent clinical thinking! Elevating the head of the bed helps blood flow smoothly out of the head (venous return), preventing fluid backup and keeping pressure low.

question: You notice clear fluid leaking from a head dressing after a patient's craniotomy. What is this fluid likely to be?
explanation: Spot on, future nurse! Clear or yellowish fluid leaking from a cranial site could be cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). This is an urgent finding that you must report to the surgeon right away.

question: Which member of the healthcare team is best at helping a patient relearn everyday tasks like bathing, dressing, and cooking?
explanation: You're doing fantastic! Occupational therapists focus on daily 'occupations'—helping patients gain independence with self-care tasks so they can get back to living their lives.

question: What is a major safety worry for a patient dealing with dysphagia (difficulty swallowing) after brain surgery?
explanation: You nailed it! When swallowing is weak, food or saliva can slip down the windpipe into the lungs. This puts the patient at high risk for a dangerous lung infection called aspiration pneumonia.
